triage.name: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infections
triage.reason: Classic infant bronchiolitis with wheeze, tachypnea and feeding difficulty; diagnosis and severity assessment are core pediatric skills.

demographics: Nearly all children are infected by age 2
Infants and young children account for most severe pediatric disease
Adults 65 and older have the highest adult hospitalization rates
In the US, infections cluster in fall through spring (RSV season)

risk_factors.text: Infancy, especially under 6 months of age
Chronic lung disease such as asthma, COPD or bronchopulmonary dysplasia
Congenital heart disease or heart failure
Residence in a nursing home or other congregate living setting
Household or daycare exposure to someone with a cold or RSV
Neuromuscular disorder with difficulty clearing secretions

comorbidities: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia or other chronic lung disease of prematurity
social_history: Daycare attendance or older siblings at home
Nursing home or assisted living residence

chief_complaints.text: My nose is runny and I keep coughing
My baby is breathing fast and wheezing
My child is not eating or drinking well
I feel short of breath and worn out

hpi.onset: Gradual, starting 4 to 6 days after exposure with nasal congestion and runny nose
hpi.duration: Symptoms peak around days 3 to 5 and usually resolve in 1 to 2 weeks; cough can linger longer
hpi.progression: Begins as a mild cold with congestion and cough, then in more severe cases progresses over several days to wheezing, fast breathing, and difficulty feeding or shortness of breath
hpi.location: Upper airway at first, then chest and lower airways
hpi.quality: Clear runny nose and sneezing, followed by a dry or wet cough and audible wheezing
hpi.severity: Mild in most people; moderate to severe in infants, older adults, and those with chronic heart or lung disease or weakened immunity
hpi.timing: Continuous, worse at night and with feeding or activity

associated_symptoms.text: Irritability or decreased activity in infants

pertinent_negatives: Barking cough with a hoarse voice
Sudden onset of symptoms within hours
High fever with severe body aches
Vomiting and diarrhea as the main symptoms
Sick contacts with a known strep or influenza diagnosis

atypical.how_it_differs: Very young infants may have no classic cold symptoms and instead present with irritability, decreased activity, poor feeding, and trouble breathing; apnea can be the first sign.
Symptoms may be milder or atypical, with low-grade fever, confusion, or worsening of underlying heart or lung disease rather than prominent wheezing.
Illness can be more severe and prolonged, with higher viral loads and progression to pneumonia; shedding may last weeks.
Older children often have a mild cold or tracheobronchitis rather than bronchiolitis, and may wheeze if they have asthma.

general.mild: Alert, playful or interactive, feeding well, no respiratory distress
general.moderate: Mildly irritable or tired, feeding less than usual, mild tachypnea with intercostal retractions
general.severe: Irritable or lethargic, poor feeding, marked tachypnea with nasal flaring and retractions, audible wheeze
general.critical: Lethargic or unresponsive, unable to feed, grunting, apnea or cyanosis, impending respiratory failure

findings.maneuver: Inspect the nasal passages and nares
findings.finding: Clear rhinorrhea and congested nasal mucosa

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oropharynx with a tongue blade
findings.finding: Mild pharyngeal erythema without exudate or tonsillar enlargement

findings.maneuver: Perform pneumatic otoscopy of both tympanic membranes
findings.finding: Bulging, erythematous, immobile tympanic membrane suggesting acute otitis media

findings.maneuver: Count the respiratory rate for a full 60 seconds while the patient is calm
findings.finding: Elevated respiratory rate for age

findings.maneuver: Auscultate all lung fields with the bell and diaphragm during quiet breathing
findings.finding: Diffuse expiratory wheezing, often with a prolonged expiratory phase
Fine inspiratory crackles

findings.maneuver: Listen for the ratio of inspiration to expiration
findings.finding: Prolonged expiratory phase

findings.maneuver: Observe the chest wall for suprasternal, intercostal, or subcostal indrawing
findings.finding: Intercostal, subcostal, or suprasternal retractions
Nasal flaring with each breath

findings.maneuver: Listen for expiratory grunting without a stethoscope
findings.finding: Audible expiratory grunting

findings.maneuver: Observe the head and neck during breathing
findings.finding: Head bobbing with each breath (infants)

findings.maneuver: Observe breathing for 20 seconds or more, especially in infants under 2 months
findings.finding: Pauses in breathing lasting 20 seconds or more, or shorter pauses with bradycardia or cyanosis

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips, tongue, and nail beds
findings.finding: Central cyanosis

findings.maneuver: Assess mucous membranes, skin turgor, and fontanelle
findings.finding: Dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor, or sunken fontanelle

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart and count the rate for 60 seconds
findings.finding: Heart rate above the normal range for age

findings.maneuver: Auscultate for murmurs, gallops, and rubs
findings.finding: Normal S1 and S2 without murmur or gallop

findings.maneuver: Listen over the trachea and neck during quiet breathing
findings.finding: No inspiratory stridor at rest

findings.maneuver: Observe swallowing and ask about drooling
findings.finding: No drooling or difficulty swallowing

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient's overall interaction and tone
findings.finding: Alert and interactive without toxic appearance

labs.caveat: Viral illness usually gives a normal or mildly elevated count; marked leukocytosis suggests bacterial superinfection.
Lymphocytosis is typical of viral infection but is nonspecific.
Mildly elevated in uncomplicated RSV; higher values raise concern for bacterial pneumonia.
Low values support a viral cause and argue against bacterial pneumonia.
Hyponatremia can occur with SIADH in severe bronchiolitis.
Low bicarbonate suggests metabolic acidosis from respiratory distress or dehydration.
Elevated from dehydration and poor oral intake.
Rises with dehydration or acute kidney injury.
Rising CO2 in a tiring patient signals impending respiratory failure.
Elevated with severe hypoxemia or shock.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia appropriate for age and fever
Sinus rhythm
No specific ECG pattern for RSV; ECG is not part of routine workup and is done only to evaluate hypoxia, tachycardia, or suspected myocarditis

imaging.preferred_when: When pneumonia or another complication is suspected, or the diagnosis is unclear

findings.text: Peribronchial cuffing and increased perihilar markings
Patchy or diffuse airspace opacities (viral pneumonia)
Focal lobar consolidation suggesting bacterial superinfection

imaging.preferred_when: Rarely needed; considered in immunocompromised or severely ill adults when complications are unclear

findings.text: Tree-in-bud nodularity or bronchial wall thickening

imaging.preferred_when: Point-of-care assessment of consolidation or effusion when available

initial.why: Confirms RSV and identifies other viruses such as influenza or SARS-CoV-2 that change management
Detects hypoxemia and guides oxygen therapy

initial.only_if: pneumonia is suspected (abnormal vitals, focal exam findings, or worsening course)
poor feeding, vomiting, or dehydration is present
bacterial infection is suspected (high fever, toxic appearance, focal findings)

confirmatory.why: The reference standard for confirming RSV infection

supporting.why: Supports inflammation and helps assess bacterial superinfection
Low values favor a viral cause
supporting.only_if: distinguishing viral from bacterial pneumonia is uncertain
severe respiratory distress or impending respiratory failure

not_indicated.why: Not routine in typical bronchiolitis; does not change management unless pneumonia is suspected
Not routine when the patient is feeding and hydrated
Not needed in mild or moderate illness
No role unless shock or severe hypoxemia is present
Not routine; reserved for uncertain bacterial coinfection
Rarely changes management and exposes the patient to radiation

decision_points: Use the rapid respiratory viral panel in patients who are hospitalized, immunocompromised, or when the result changes management (for example, influenza antiviral therapy).
Assess severity with respiratory rate, work of breathing, feeding, and oxygen saturation; these guide admission and oxygen therapy.
Do not order a chest x-ray routinely; order it when pneumonia or another complication is suspected.
Consider bacterial superinfection when fever is high or persistent, the patient is toxic-appearing, or focal consolidation is present.

differential.name: Influenza
differential.why_considered: Seasonal viral illness with fever, cough, and nasal congestion in the same fall-to-spring window as RSV
differential.trigger: Abrupt onset of high fever with prominent myalgias and headache during influenza season

history: Sudden onset over hours rather than the gradual 4 to 6 day RSV prodrome
Severe body aches, headache, and chills
Wheezing and feeding difficulty are less prominent in older children and adults
exam: High fever with a toxic or markedly fatigued appearance
Diffuse wheezing and marked retractions are less typical
labs: Rapid influenza antigen or PCR positive on nasopharyngeal swab
Respiratory viral panel negative for RSV
imaging: Chest x-ray usually normal unless viral pneumonia develops

differential.name: SARS-CoV-2 infection
differential.why_considered: Overlapping cough, fever, and respiratory distress during respiratory virus season
differential.trigger: Known COVID-19 exposure or a household cluster of respiratory illness with loss of taste or smell

history: Loss of taste or smell
Exposure to a confirmed COVID-19 case
Wheezing in an infant is less typical
exam: Findings range from normal to severe hypoxemia with minimal auscultatory findings
Diffuse wheeze is less common than in RSV bronchiolitis
labs: Respiratory viral panel negative for RSV
imaging: Chest x-ray may show peripheral or basilar opacities
CT chest may show peripheral ground-glass opacities

differential.name: Human metapneumovirus infection
differential.why_considered: Nearly identical bronchiolitis syndrome with wheeze, tachypnea, and feeding difficulty in young children

history: Indistinguishable clinically from RSV
Same seasonal pattern and age distribution
exam: Diffuse wheezing and retractions identical to RSV bronchiolitis
labs: Respiratory viral panel positive for human metapneumovirus and negative for RSV
imaging: Chest x-ray findings of hyperinflation and peribronchial cuffing are the same

differential.name: Parainfluenza virus infection
differential.why_considered: Common cause of croup and lower respiratory infection in young children with cough and stridor

history: Barking cough and hoarse voice
Stridor worse at night
exam: Suprasternal retractions with a hoarse cry
labs: Respiratory viral panel positive for parainfluenza and negative for RSV
imaging: Neck x-ray may show subglottic narrowing (steeple sign)

differential.name: Bacterial pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Fever, cough, and tachypnea with abnormal lung findings in a child or older adult
differential.trigger: High or persistent fever, focal crackles, or toxic appearance

history: Fever may be higher and more persistent
Productive cough with purulent sputum in older patients
Less prominent wheezing and sneezing
exam: Focal crackles or dullness rather than diffuse wheeze
labs: Respiratory viral panel may be negative or show a coinfection
imaging: Focal lobar consolidation on chest x-ray

differential.name: Asthma exacerbation
differential.why_considered: Wheezing, cough, and increased work of breathing in a child or adult

history: Recurrent episodes of wheeze triggered by allergens, exercise, or cold air
Known asthma diagnosis
No preceding cold symptoms in some cases
exam: Eczema or allergic rhinitis may be present
labs: Respiratory viral panel negative for RSV
imaging: Chest x-ray usually normal or hyperinflated

differential.name: Foreign body aspiration
differential.why_considered: Sudden onset of cough, wheeze, or respiratory distress in a young child
differential.trigger: Abrupt onset of choking or coughing while eating or playing, with unilateral wheeze

history: Sudden onset during eating or playing
No preceding runny nose or fever
Witnessed choking episode
exam: Unilateral wheeze or decreased breath sounds
Stridor may be present if the object is in the upper airway
imaging: Chest x-ray may show unilateral hyperinflation, mediastinal shift, or a radiopaque object
CT or bronchoscopy may be needed if suspicion is high

differential.name: Pertussis
differential.why_considered: Prolonged cough illness with post-tussive vomiting in infants and older children

history: Paroxysmal cough lasting weeks
Inspiratory whoop
Post-tussive vomiting
Cough worse at night
exam: Whoop may be absent in infants
labs: PCR or culture positive for Bordetella pertussis
imaging: Chest x-ray usually normal or shows mild perihilar markings

severity.mild: Upper respiratory cold: clear rhinorrhea, sneezing, mild cough, low-grade or no fever, feeding and activity preserved, no respiratory distress, oxygen saturation 95% or higher on room air
severity.moderate: Lower respiratory involvement: tachypnea for age, mild retractions, audible or auscultated wheeze, decreased feeding, oxygen saturation 92 to 96% on room air, no apnea
severity.severe: Marked respiratory distress: tachypnea with nasal flaring and intercostal or subcostal retractions, grunting, poor feeding, dehydration, oxygen saturation 88 to 92% on room air, may require supplemental oxygen and hospitalization
severity.critical: Impending or overt respiratory failure: apnea, cyanosis, lethargy, grunting, oxygen saturation below 88% on room air, rising PaCO2, or need for mechanical ventilation; can be life-threatening

red_flags.finding: Apnea or pauses in breathing lasting 20 seconds or more
red_flags.meaning: Impending respiratory failure, especially in infants under 2 months; requires immediate evaluation and monitoring

red_flags.finding: Central cyanosis or oxygen saturation below 90% on room air
red_flags.meaning: Severe hypoxemia; needs supplemental oxygen and possible escalation of care

red_flags.finding: Grunting, nasal flaring, or marked retractions
red_flags.meaning: Severe increased work of breathing; indicates impending respiratory failure
Systemic decompensation; may require intravenous fluids and hospitalization

red_flags.finding: High or persistent fever with focal lung findings
red_flags.meaning: Possible bacterial superinfection such as pneumonia; consider chest x-ray and antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Rising PaCO2 or respiratory acidosis on blood gas

complications.name: Bronchiolitis
clues: Wheezing and crackles in an infant

complications.name: Viral pneumonia
clues: Patchy or diffuse opacities on chest x-ray

complications.name: Bacterial superinfection (pneumonia or otitis media)
clues: Ear pain or bulging tympanic membrane

complications.name: Apnea
clues: Pauses in breathing with bradycardia or cyanosis

complications.name: Hyponatremia from SIADH
clues: Confusion or seizures in severe cases

complications.name: Worsening of underlying asthma or COPD
clues: Increased wheeze and shortness of breath

complications.name: Worsening of heart failure
clues: New or worsening edema and dyspnea

special_populations.differences: Highest risk for severe disease, especially under 6 months and those born prematurely. Apnea can be the first sign. Very young infants may present only with irritability, decreased activity, and poor feeding without classic cough or wheeze.
Older children often have a mild cold or tracheobronchitis rather than bronchiolitis. Those with asthma may wheeze prominently and respond to bronchodilators.
Symptoms may be milder or atypical, with low-grade fever, confusion, or worsening of underlying heart or lung disease rather than prominent wheezing. Higher risk of hospitalization and death.
Illness can be more severe and prolonged, with higher viral loads, progression to pneumonia, and viral shedding lasting weeks. Consider prolonged isolation and antiviral discussion with specialists.
RSV can cause more severe respiratory illness in pregnancy. Maternal vaccination between 32 and 36 weeks gestation protects the newborn for the first 6 months of life.
Poor glycemic control may worsen with infection; monitor blood glucose closely during acute illness.
May increase risk of severe lower respiratory infection and hypoxemia; monitor respiratory status closely.

key_questions.question: How did the illness start, and how has it changed over the past few days?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset of runny nose and cough 4 to 6 days after exposure, worsening over days 3 to 5 toward wheezing and fast breathing

key_questions.question: Is the patient breathing fast, working hard to breathe, or having pauses in breathing?
key_questions.looking_for: Tachypnea, retractions, nasal flaring, grunting, or apnea, especially in infants under 2 months

key_questions.question: How is feeding and fluid intake compared with normal?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, or refusal to drink, indicating dehydration and need for admission

key_questions.question: Is there any wheezing or noisy breathing?
key_questions.looking_for: Audible or auscultated wheeze with prolonged expiration, typical of bronchiolitis

key_questions.question: Any fever, and how high has it been?
key_questions.looking_for: Low-grade to moderate fever; high or persistent fever raises concern for bacterial superinfection

key_questions.question: Any ear pain, ear pulling, or discharge?
key_questions.looking_for: Otitis media as a complication, common in young children with RSV

key_questions.question: Has the patient been around anyone with a cold, or is there a daycare or school outbreak?
key_questions.looking_for: Sick contacts or group exposure during RSV season (fall through spring)

key_questions.question: Was the patient born prematurely, or do they have chronic lung, heart, or immune problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Risk factors for severe disease: prematurity, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, congenital heart disease, immunosuppression, cystic fibrosis, neuromuscular disease

key_questions.question: Does the patient take any immunosuppressive medications?
key_questions.looking_for: Corticosteroids, tacrolimus, cyclosporine, mycophenolate, azathioprine, methotrexate, or rituximab, which increase risk of severe and prolonged illness

key_questions.question: Has the patient received an RSV vaccine or monoclonal antibody (nirsevimab or palivizumab)?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunization status; prior protection lowers but does not eliminate risk

key_questions.question: Any barking cough, hoarse voice, drooling, or trouble swallowing?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; these point to croup, epiglottitis, or another diagnosis rather than RSV

key_questions.question: Any sudden choking episode while eating or playing?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; a witnessed choking event with unilateral wheeze suggests foreign body aspiration

reasoning_points: Gradual cold-like prodrome with runny nose and cough that worsens over several days
Wheezing with tachypnea and increased work of breathing in an infant or high-risk adult
Poor feeding or dehydration in an infant
Risk factors such as infancy, prematurity, age 65 or older, chronic lung or heart disease, or immunosuppression
Presentation during RSV season (fall through spring) with sick contacts
Positive rapid respiratory viral panel or PCR for RSV on a nasopharyngeal swab
Chest x-ray findings of hyperinflation and peribronchial cuffing when imaging is obtained
Absence of features pointing to influenza, COVID-19, bacterial pneumonia, croup, asthma, or foreign body aspiration

easy: Infant under 1 year with classic runny nose, cough, and wheeze
Presentation during RSV season with a sick contact
Diffuse wheezing with tachypnea and mild retractions
medium: Older adult with low-grade fever, cough, and worsening of underlying COPD or heart failure rather than prominent wheeze
Infant with apnea or poor feeding but minimal cough or wheeze
Child with fever and ear pain suggesting otitis media complicating RSV
Need to distinguish RSV from influenza or COVID-19 during respiratory virus season
hard: Very young infant under 2 months presenting only with irritability, decreased activity, and apnea
Immunocompromised patient with prolonged, severe illness and progression to pneumonia
Patient with focal crackles and high fever suggesting bacterial superinfection rather than viral bronchiolitis
Toddler with sudden unilateral wheeze raising concern for foreign body aspiration
Pregnant patient with severe respiratory illness requiring assessment of both maternal and fetal status
